passage: The lift doors were closing when the director asked, "Who came up with the churn analysis?" Nikita opened her mouth. Tanuja had built the model over two weekends, and Nikita had only made the slides. For a second the word "I" sat ready on her tongue, because promotion talks were next month. "Tanuja built the model. I turned it into slides," she said instead, holding the door. The director looked at them both. "Good. Put both names on the summary." Nikita's heart was pounding, half regret and half relief. In the lift she told herself it had cost her nothing yet, and knew that was not quite true.

qa.q: Who built the churn analysis model?
qa.a: Tanuja built the model over two weekends.

qa.q: What was Nikita tempted to do, and what was on her mind?
qa.a: She felt torn, tempted to say "I" and take the credit because promotion talks were next month.

qa.q: Why does naming who did what matter for the team later?
qa.a: It builds trust, and the director asked for both names on the summary, so both people are recognised. 🙂

qa.q: How might Tanuja have felt hearing Nikita's answer?
qa.a: Tanuja probably felt relieved and valued, since the real work was named instead of being passed off.

grounding: A colleague is tempted to present shared work as her own but names who did what.
